attempts.label: CRCNS:ac-1
attempts.entry_title: Long-lasting context dependence in rat auditory cortex (Asari & Zador 2009)
attempts.summary: The paper's central finding held in this data: A1 responses depend on the preceding sounds for seconds, while in the thalamus (MGB) the effect fades fast. Its timescale did not match, as the context-dependent power decays with a time constant of 1.74 to 1.78 s against the paper's 1.04 s; the predictability bound missed on its time constant too, and the STRF result failed because a longer window gave a small significant gain. Amplitude and frequency changes outlasted modulation and higher-order changes, but gave smaller effects than natural sounds, on property sets rebuilt because the paper does not list them. The synaptic conductance findings could not be tested, as the data set holds no voltage-clamp recordings.
attempts.description: Tests the findings of Asari and Zador (2009) on CRCNS ac-1, which holds their in vivo whole-cell recordings in rat A1 and cell-attached recordings in MGB, with natural and synthetic sound sequences, and the analysis code of the paper. It measures how long the response to a probe depends on the preceding sound, the response predictability without context, the dependence on sound properties, and the fast decay in thalamus. The voltage-clamp recordings of Figures 5 and 6 are not in the data set.

notebooks.title: Reproducing Asari & Zador (2009) from CRCNS ac-1
Figure 4 STRF and LN models of Wehr's recordings from CRCNS ac-1

outcomes.statement: Of 194 A1 cells recorded in current clamp, 123 met the analysis criterion (39 tested with natural sounds, 14 with TORCs, 6 with DMRs, 39 with modulated harmonic tones, 27 with modulated colored noise); 14 of 42 voltage-clamped cells and 14 of 16 MGB cells were analysed.
outcomes.source: Methods, Electrophysiology, paragraphs 2 and 3; Table 1
outcomes.quote: All together, we recorded from 194 cells in 139 animals in current-clamp mode, of which 123 cells met our criterion for the analysis ... Of these, 39 cells were examined with natural sound ensembles, 14 cells with ensembles of temporally orthogonal ripple combinations, 6 cells with ensembles of dynamic moving ripples, 39 cells with ensembles of modulated harmonic tones, and 27 cells with ensembles of modulated colored noise ensembles
outcomes.notes: Under the paper's rule (at least two conditioning stimuli, at least 4 trials in A1 and 10 in MGB), the natural sound group of Summary.mat gives 305 probes in 39 cells and the MGB group 93 probes in 14 cells, with silence counted as a context or not; these match. All A1 whole-cell recordings with sequences give 133 cells (644 probes) against the paper's 123: the 39 natural sound cells and 96 synthetic sound cells, 2 of them in both. By ensemble, TORC (14 cells) and MCN (27) match, DMR gives 15 cells against 6 and MHT 26 against 39, and 14 cells were tested with SoundTrans variants of natural sounds, which the paper's list does not name. Each of the 96 synthetic cells has at least one probe tested with a one-property set; the notebook lists them with the properties tested. The listing does not show which 123 cells the paper counted, so the 10 extra cells cannot be named. The data set holds no voltage-clamp recording (every file is whole-cell current clamp in mV or cell-attached), so the 29 voltage-clamp probes in 14 cells are recorded as 0; that part of the claim cannot be tested here. The data set holds 145 A1 whole-cell cells and 14 MGB cells in all, against 194 and 16 recorded.
deviations: Probe responses are formed as the paper's analysis script asari/Tools/CxtDep.m (in the data set) forms them, a detail the Methods leave open. Each sequence presentation is cut at its trigger, fragments at the sum of the rounded durations before them, the first 'Effective repeats' presentations are used, silence is a context (the last 4 s before a sequence) and a probe (the first 2.5 s after it), and each context is cut to the smallest number of trials.

outcomes.statement: Firing rates were low in A1 (spontaneous 0.47 +/- 0.61 Hz, evoked 0.57 +/- 0.77 Hz, mean +/- SD, 194 cells) and high in MGB (spontaneous 0.78 +/- 1.25 Hz, evoked 11.4 +/- 16.9 Hz, 16 cells).
outcomes.source: Methods, Analysis, paragraphs 2 and 3; Results, Context dependence, paragraph 1; Results, Subcortical contribution to context dependence, paragraph 2
outcomes.quote: Because of the low firing rates in A1 (spontaneous, 0.47 ... 0.61 Hz; evoked, 0.57 ... 0.77 Hz ... 194 cells ... Sufficiently high firing rates in MGB allowed us to analyze the context dependence at the spike level (spontaneous, 0.78 ... 1.25 Hz; evoked, 11.4 ... 16.9 Hz
outcomes.notes: Mean over cells, each cell pooling its files, under 32 readings (A1 detector, MGB detector, all files or context files, spontaneous window silences or 1-s pre-stimulus baseline, evoked window stimulus periods or probe periods). None has all four means within tolerance. A1 with a 10 mV/ms upstroke detector over all files is 0.474 Hz spontaneous (SD 0.603, silences) and 0.695 Hz evoked (SD 0.893; 0.722 over the probe periods), against 0.47 (0.61) and 0.57 (0.77); the starting values of the code's manual detector give 0.16 to 0.23 Hz. MGB with the code's automatic detector is 0.618 Hz spontaneous (silences; 0.72 to 0.82 Hz with the baseline, within tolerance) and 4.99 to 5.07 Hz evoked (SD 11.5), and with half its threshold 0.77 to 1.04 Hz and 7.07 to 7.15 Hz, against 0.78 (1.25) and 11.4 (16.9). A1 means are below 1 Hz in every reading, and A1 below 1 Hz with the MGB evoked mean above 5 Hz, the criterion's rule for partial, holds in 28 of the 32 readings. With the code's own MGB detector it rests on a margin of 0.03 to 0.07 Hz over 5 Hz (6 of its 8 readings; the other 2 give 4.99 Hz); it is met by a wide margin only with half that detector's threshold, a choice made here. The data set has 145 A1 and 14 MGB cells, not 194 and 16.
deviations: The paper does not say how A1 spikes were detected; its code (ViewResp.m, GetSpikes.m) detects them by hand for whole-cell data. Two detectors are run, the starting values of the code's manual detector (threshold 1 on its high-passed trace) and a 10 mV/ms upstroke with a 2-ms dead time (a standard choice). MGB spikes use the code's automatic detector (high-pass filter, threshold two thirds of the largest filtered value), which ViewResp.m applies to cell-attached data; the Methods say only 'a high-pass filter and thresholding'. A second MGB reading uses half of that threshold.

The criterion's window readings are all run. Spontaneous periods are the silences between stimuli (split as GetEvoked.m does) or the 1 s before each stimulus, cut to the silence before it (a standard choice for the pre-stimulus baseline); evoked periods are every stimulus period or the probe periods analysed (the fragments of the first 'Effective repeats' presentations of each sequence). The file readings are all of a cell's files (with tuning curves) or its sequence files only.

outcomes.statement: The example A1 neuron of Figure 2 had high trial-to-trial reliability (correlation across trials 0.74 +/- 0.08 for the shown probe and 0.61 +/- 0.07 over the seven natural sound fragments tested), and the mean correlation over the population was 0.31 +/- 0.09.
outcomes.source: Results, Context dependence, paragraph 2; Figure 2A legend
outcomes.quote: the correlation coefficient of the response traces across trials in a given context was 0.61 ... 0.07 (mean ... SD) for the seven natural sound fragments tested in this cell. The reliability varied within a given neuron as a function of the stimuli tested and across neurons; the mean correlation coefficient was 0.31 ... 0.09
outcomes.notes: Correlation between the trials of one context over the probe period, mean over pairs of trials, averaged over contexts. Over the 39 cells (cell means) it is 0.310 +/- 0.092 and over the 305 probes 0.319 +/- 0.129 (paper 0.31 +/- 0.09). Of the five recordings with seven natural sound fragments and six effective repeats, 20051222-ha1-001-002 gives 0.611 +/- 0.081 over its seven probes and 0.737 for its best probe (paper 0.61 +/- 0.07 and 0.74); the other four give 0.244 to 0.309. The leave-one-out reading (each trial against the mean of the others) gives 0.437 +/- 0.098 over cells, outside tolerance.

outcomes.statement: In an example A1 neuron, changing the conditioning stimulus changed the response to the probe for about 4 s; responses did not differ between 2 and 4 s after probe onset and diverged again after about 4 s.
outcomes.source: Figure 2B and 2D; Results, Context dependence, paragraph 3
outcomes.quote: Interestingly, context-induced differences could sometimes be intermittent; the three average response traces showed no difference in the interval 2 to 4 s after the onset of the probe, but diverged again after about 4 s

statistics.test: Kruskal-Wallis test at each time point, P < 0.01 for at least 5 ms
statistics.n: one cell, one probe in three contexts (6 repeats shown for one context in Figure 2A)

outcomes.notes: 20 candidate probes (cells with seven fragments, contexts silence and two fragments, 6 trials per context). Probe 4 of 20060105-ha1-001-002 (contexts 2, 3 and silence) meets the criterion: significant periods at 0.67 to 1.36 s, none from 2 to 4 s, and one at 4.00 to 4.06 s. It is a selected example (1 of 20 candidates), and its late period lasts 60 ms. In 20051222-ha1-001-002, the cell whose reliability matches the example, probe 4 is significant up to 1.60 s, not from 1.60 to 3.97 s, and again from 3.97 to 4.60 s; its run at 3.97 to 4.01 s starts inside the 2 to 4 s window, so it fails the strict test. Probe 4 is the probe of that cell with reliability 0.737 (the 0.74 of Figure 2A), and the Figure 2B legend says its red trace is the context shown in A, so that probe is most likely the paper's example. The passing probe is from a cell with mean reliability 0.309, which is not the paper's example cell. The criterion does not use this link and accepts any of the 20 candidates, so the outcome follows it as written; the link is a question for a reader (questions/asari-2009.yaml). The notebook lists every significant period of each candidate and the reliability of each probe of 20051222-ha1-001-002. 17 of 305 natural sound probes have a significant period later than 4 s.

Each sequence presentation is cut at its trigger, fragments at the sum of the rounded durations before them, the first 'Effective repeats' presentations are used, silence is a context (the last 4 s before a sequence) and a probe (the first 2.5 s after it), and each context is cut to the smallest number of trials.

The significance measure follows the Methods (Kruskal-Wallis at every 0.1-ms point, P < 0.01 for at least 5 ms, noise floor from 1000 shuffles of trials across contexts) with the details of KWtest in CxtDep.m: ordinal ranks with ties broken by trial order, no tie correction, a run kept when its last and first points are at least 50 samples apart, and whole trials shuffled. A variant with average ranks gives the same count.

outcomes.source: Figure 3A legend, bottom panel; Results, Context dependence, paragraph 7
outcomes.inferred: The fit values are in the Figure 3A legend, where the symbols are garbled in the text extraction (read as alpha1 = 0.17, tau1 = 0.20 s, alpha2 = 0.09, tau2 = 0.90 s, kappa = mean noise floor = 2.8 x 10^-3); the Results restate the long constant as about one second.
outcomes.notes: Eq. 44 with the constant fixed at the mean noise floor of the fit range. Two exponentials are selected by the paper's rule under every reading with silence counted. Over all probes, fitted to 4.72 s, the values are 0.149, 0.252 s, 0.079, 0.968 s with a noise floor of 2.5e-3; only the slow constant is within tolerance. Over the running probes they are 0.159, 0.265 s, 0.068, 1.075 s with 2.8e-3; the fast size and the noise floor are within tolerance. The fast constant is 0.25 to 0.27 s in every reading, against 0.20 s. Without silence as a context one exponential is selected. The slow constant is between 0.5 and 2 s, which meets the rule for partial.

outcomes.source: Figure 3B legend, bottom panel; Results, Context dependence, paragraph 7
outcomes.quote: For both measures there was a long decay constant of about one second
outcomes.notes: Q(t) of Eq. 20 with the denominator smoothed over [0, 2t], one exponential with constant 0. With silence counted the size is 0.464 to 0.468 and the time constant 1.74 to 1.78 s over the four readings of denominator and fit range; without silence 0.445 to 0.450 and 1.29 to 1.33 s. The size is within tolerance of 0.49 under every reading and the time constant is outside tolerance of 1.04 s under every reading, so no reading meets the criterion, which gives no rule for partial. Q averages 0.66 over the first 100 ms and 0.12 from 3 to 4 s: the effect is present with the paper's size but decays more slowly.

outcomes.statement: The trial-to-trial noise autocorrelation and the autocorrelation of spontaneous activity decay within about 100 ms, much faster than the second-long timescale of context dependence in A1.
outcomes.source: Methods, Analysis, Timescale of intrinsic membrane properties; Results, Context dependence, paragraph 7
outcomes.quote: we found that ... had a sharp peak with a rapid decay (within ... 100 ms; data not shown), much faster than the slow timescale identified in neural responses in area A1
outcomes.notes: The mean normalized autocorrelation of the trial-to-trial noise (Eq. 14 residuals, 305 probes) falls below 1/e at 73 ms and below 0.1 at 116 ms; per probe the 1/e lag has median 72 ms and maximum 152 ms. Over the intersequence silences of 46 recordings the spontaneous autocorrelation falls below 1/e at 78 ms (77 ms without the first 1 s) and below 0.1 at 124 ms. Both 1/e lags are under 150 ms and under a third of 1.04 s.
deviations: Probe responses are formed as the paper's analysis script asari/Tools/CxtDep.m (in the data set) forms them, a detail the Methods leave open. Each trace is mean-removed before its autocorrelation, and per-probe autocorrelations are normalized at lag 0 before averaging (Eq. 45 normalizes by the noise variance).

outcomes.source: Results, Relation to response predictability, paragraph 4; Figure 4 legend
outcomes.quote: shows that no model can capture more than a half

Unsmoothed, 1 + alpha1 is 0.50 (silence counted) or 0.53 to 0.54 (not), within tolerance of 0.51, with time constants of 1.46 to 1.92 s. The mean of the smoothed ratio over the first 100 ms is 0.50 with silence counted and 0.57 without (unsmoothed 0.39 and 0.44). The bound near onset is about half, as the paper says, but the time constant is outside tolerance of 1.04 s under every reading, so the criterion's joint test fails; the criterion gives no rule for partial.

outcomes.statement: Linear STRF models of 20 A1 cells from Machens et al. (2004) predicted less than about 20% of the predictable response power, and extending the window from 180 ms to about 4 s did not improve them significantly, with or without a static nonlinearity; the LN model did only slightly better.
outcomes.source: Results, Relation to response predictability, paragraph 5; Figure 4; Discussion, Context dependence and model construction, paragraph 4
outcomes.quote: The performance of STRF-based models was in general unsatisfactory ... consistent with previous work (Ahrens et al. 2008; Machens et al. 2004; Sahani and Linden 2003). The performance did not improve significantly, however, when we extended the window length
outcomes.notes: Wehr's recordings of Machens et al. (2004) are in the data set (wehr/ in crcns-ac1.zip). Of its 25 cells, 16 have natural sounds presented at least twice, which Eq. 52 needs; they are used (the paper used 20 and does not list them). Main reading (10-ms Hann window, contiguous folds): mean validation performance over cells 0.178 to 0.207 for STRF and 0.165 to 0.209 for LN across the nine windows (training 0.232 to 0.388), so at most 0.22 at every window. Extending the window from 180 to 4052 ms raises the validation performance by 0.030 for STRF (one-sided Wilcoxon p = 0.011) and 0.025 for LN (p = 0.042); with the 20-ms window p = 0.0065 and 0.019. With whole stimuli as folds the improvement is not significant (p = 0.12 and 0.088), but the mean LN validation performance reaches 0.241 at 3540 ms. No reading meets both parts of the criterion, which gives no rule for partial. The performance is low, near the paper's 20%; the part of the statement that a longer window does not help holds only with folds made of whole stimuli. The LN model is not better than the STRF on average (mean gain -0.010). In one cell (20020602-mw-001) no model predicts (STRF performance near 0, LN -0.574 at 180 ms and -0.713 at 4052 ms, best ridge at the end of the grid in 22 of its 27 fits). Two of these statements rest on that cell, the LN model not being better and the performance being at most 0.22 at every window. Without it (15 cells, main reading) the LN model is better by 0.025 on average and the mean validation performance reaches 0.222 for STRF and 0.253 for LN, above 0.22; the longer window still helps significantly (p = 0.011 for STRF, 0.0075 for LN), so the outcome is the same.
deviations: Assumption. The paper's 20 cells are not listed (Methods, Neural encoding models, 'the recording data (20 cells) from the previous work'). Every cell with at least one natural sound presented at least twice is used (16 cells), with those sounds only, as Eq. 52 needs two trials.

Spectrogram (Eq. 47) with a Hann window of 10 ms (main) or 20 ms (the criterion's readings), power in third-octave bands from 400 Hz (17 bands, to 20.3 kHz), floored 100 dB below the cell's largest value before the logarithm (a standard choice), each channel centred over the cell's stimuli; silence before stimulus onset. Responses are the membrane potential with spikes clipped by a 10-ms median filter (ViewResponse.m), in 4-ms bins, centred per trial; the 10-kHz reading of the criterion does not apply, as the responses are sampled at 4 kHz.

Ridge regression with 10-fold cross-validation, the ridge parameter chosen by the best mean validation performance over folds (STRFanalysis.m) from 17 values spanning 1e-7 to 10 times the largest eigenvalue of S'S (a standard choice; interior in 410 of 432 fits). Folds are contiguous blocks (main) or whole stimuli (fewer than 10 folds for cells with fewer than 10 stimuli). The lowess nonlinearity (5% span, five robustness iterations) is evaluated on 60 points of the linear estimate and interpolated (a standard approximation).

Assumption. 'Did not improve significantly' is tested, as the claims file fixes it, by a one-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test over cells of validation performance at 4052 against 180 ms; a Friedman test over the nine windows is shown and does not decide.

outcomes.statement: In an example voltage-clamped A1 cell, excitatory and inhibitory conductances evoked by the probe decayed within about 100 ms in all six contexts, yet their variance over contexts lasted long, longer for inhibition than for excitation.
outcomes.source: Results, Context dependence of synaptic conductances, paragraph 2; Figure 5D to 5G
outcomes.quote: In all cases we examined, both excitatory and inhibitory conductances elicited in this cell decayed rapidly within about 100 ms, yet the context dependence measured as the variance of the conductances lasted long, especially for the inhibitory conductance in this example
outcomes.notes: No voltage-clamp recording is in the data set. Every one of Asari's 346 files is a whole-cell current-clamp recording in mV (A1) or a cell-attached recording (MGB); none holds currents or the three holding potentials, and Summary.mat names no voltage-clamp group. The paper's 42 voltage-clamped cells are not public elsewhere as far as the paper and the data set's documentation say.

outcomes.statement: Across 29 probes in 14 voltage-clamped cells, context dependence of both excitatory and inhibitory conductances decayed with a long constant of seconds (1.22 and 2.50 s) and a short one of hundreds of milliseconds (0.14 and 0.13 s).
outcomes.source: Results, Context dependence of synaptic conductances, paragraph 3; Figure 6A and 6B
outcomes.quote: For both excitatory and inhibitory conductances, there was a long decay constant on the order of seconds
outcomes.notes: Needs the voltage-clamp recordings, which are not in the data set (see fig5-example-conductances).

outcomes.statement: In an example A1 neuron, a natural sound probe preceded by three DMR contexts that differed only in frequency band gave significant context dependence for about 4 s.
outcomes.source: Figure 7A and 7B legend
outcomes.quote: in which a natural sound stimulus probe was preceded by 3 different synthetic conditioning stimuli with different bandwidths

statistics.test: Kruskal-Wallis test at each time point, P < 0.01 for at least 5 ms
statistics.n: one cell, one probe in three contexts

outcomes.notes: No recording in the data set has DMR conditioning stimuli in 0.625-2.5, 2.5-10 and 10-40 kHz, each a single band. The notebook prints the names, descriptions, bands ('ff'), SoundTrans shifts ('df') and attenuations of every DMR, TORC and SoundTrans recording, and for each DMR a checksum of its modulation parameters (tempmod, specmod, SFtemp, SFspec, envphase, sinphase, dx). The DMR frequency variants are one DMR in different bands (one modulation checksum among the 12 stimuli of each of the 5 recordings): six 2-octave bands from 0.25 to 32 kHz in 1-octave steps, forward and time-reversed (5 recordings). The other DMR recordings hold the broad and two-band stimuli 625-10000, 1250-20000, 2500-40000 and 625-2500 with 10000-40000 Hz (5 recordings; DMRipple2.m reads the 4-element band as two bands) or amplitude variants. As a weaker check, 3 of 10 natural sound probe tests with DMR frequency variants as the only contexts (in 3 recordings) have a significant period ending at least 3.6 s after probe onset.

outcomes.statement: When only one property of synthetic conditioning stimuli varied, context dependence was found in 77 of 95 probes (81.1%, 31 cells) for amplitude, 73 of 110 (35 cells) for frequency, 62 of 96 (64.6%, 27 cells) for AM, 47 of 82 (57.3%, 25 cells) for FM and 59 of 137 (43.1%, 27 cells) for higher-order properties.
outcomes.source: Results, Relation to stimulus properties, paragraphs 2 and 3; Figure 8A
outcomes.quote: we observed context-dependent effects in 77 probes (81.1%) of 95 probes (tested in 31 cells) and in 73/110 (64.6%; 35 cells), respectively (Fig. 8A) ... Context-dependent effects were observed in 62/96 (64.6%; 27 cells) for AM modulation; in 47/82 (57.3%; 25 cells) for FM modulation; and in 59/137 (43.1%; 27 cells) for colored noise modulation
outcomes.notes: Main reading of the property sets (denominators 95, 110, 96, 82, 137, as in Table 1): significant probes are 56 (0.589) for amplitude, 62 (0.564) for frequency, 41 (0.427) for AM, 29 (0.354) for FM and 45 (0.328) for higher-order, in 30, 34, 26, 24 and 27 cells. Every count is outside tolerance of 77, 73, 62, 47 and 59. The proportions keep the order amplitude > frequency and AM > FM > higher-order, which meets the rule for partial. The order holds under the other two readings of the sets (largest set; every set), and no reading has more than one count within tolerance. findings.statement: The data set holds no voltage-clamp recording. The paper analyses 29 probes in 14 of 42 voltage-clamped A1 cells (Figures 5 and 6), but every one of Asari's 346 files is a whole-cell current-clamp recording in mV or a cell-attached recording, and Summary.mat lists only current-clamp, cell-attached and unpublished groups. The conductance findings cannot be tested.

The example recording of Figure 7 (a natural sound probe after DMRs in 0.625-2.5, 2.5-10 and 10-40 kHz) is not in the data set; no recording has DMR conditioning stimuli in those single bands. The DMR frequency variants in it are 2-octave bands from 0.25 to 32 kHz in 1-octave steps.

The data set holds 145 A1 whole-cell cells and 14 MGB cells, against the 194 current-clamp and 16 MGB cells the paper recorded. Its natural sound and MGB groups hold exactly the 39 cells with 305 probes and the 14 cells with 93 probes the paper analysed. The synthetic sound group holds 96 cells; with the natural sound group, 133 cells meet the paper's rule for analysis against its 123, and the ensembles split differently from the paper's list (DMR 15 cells against 6, MHT 26 against 39, and 14 cells with SoundTrans variants of natural sounds).

Which conditioning stimuli of a synthetic sound recording vary which sound property (the sets behind Table 1 and Figure 8) is listed in the notes of only the 19-stimulus MHT recordings. For the others it has to be rebuilt from the stimulus parameters and descriptions. Rebuilt with one test per set for AM and FM, the sets give the five probe totals of Table 1, but the split by probe type does not match: 82 of the 96 AM tests and all 82 FM tests have a natural sound probe, and only 2 recordings have MHT probes, where Table 1 gives 71 and 57 MHT-probe tests.

Summary.mat lists two cells, 20060314-ha1-001 and 20060320-ha3-003, in both the natural sound and the synthetic sound group, so their tuning-curve files are named twice. The recordings are the same files; no two files hold identical traces.

disagreements.reason: Candidate 20060105-ha1-001 probe 4 meets the rule strictly, with runs before 2 s, none from 2 to 4 s, and one at 4.00-4.06 s. 20051222-ha1-001 probe 4 fails the strict rule only because of a run at 3.97-4.01 s. The match was found among 20 candidates, so it is a selected example. Problem 8: cell 19 shows only the first 12 runs per probe.
alpha1 is 0.45-0.47 (in tolerance), but tau1 is 1.29-1.78 s against 1.04 +/- 0.10 s in all 8 readings.

No reading has tau1 within 1.04 +/- 0.10 s (range 1.46-2.81 s, plus two fits stuck at the 100 s bound). 1 + alpha1 is within 0.51 +/- 0.05 in several readings. Problem 9: two fits sit at the 100 s bound, and the smoothed Eq. 43 reaches 2.12; neither is flagged.

The notebook marks it blocked, gives no reason and has no cell for it. The archive holds wehr/Results (25 cell folders, 1626 files), wehr/Stimuli, wehr/Tools/STRFanalysis.m and ridgesvd1.m, and wehr/Contents.m gives a sample STRF pipeline. The claim is testable, so the block is not justified.

Blocked as other (search incomplete). The search reads only param.ff and collapses stimuli with set(). DMRipple2.m treats a 4-element ff as two bands. The paper makes frequency variants by shifting a generated DMR, and a shift may not show up in ff. Stimulus names and descriptions were never printed. The weaker test (a natural probe after DMR frequency contexts, significant until at least 3.6 s) could be run and was not.

As run, the amplitude interval [0.61, 0.83] and frequency interval [0.57, 0.83] exclude 1. The without-silence reference was not run and could change the outcome (problem 3), and the trial-resampling reading was not run. Problem 4: the partial check tests only that AM, FM and higher-order lie below amplitude, frequency and 1, and leaves out that amplitude and frequency reach 1.

paper_notes.statement: Question for the authors. Probes last 2 to 6 s. How do the population curves of Figures 3, 4, 8 and 9D treat times after a probe has ended: is the average at time t over all probes, an ended probe counting as zero (or not significant), or over the probes still running? The late fraction of Figure 3A matches the paper (0.252 against 0.237) only with the first reading.

Question for the authors. Which conditioning stimuli of each recording form the sets for amplitude, frequency, AM, FM and higher-order changes in Table 1 and Figure 8, and is a probe tested with several sets of one property (such as the four AM sets of the 4-by-4 AM and FM grid of the 17-stimulus MHT recordings) counted once per set? Counting each set for AM and FM and each probe once for the other properties gives the totals of Table 1 (95, 110, 96, 82, 137), but most AM and FM tests then have a natural sound probe, where Table 1 lists 71 and 57 under MHT probes.

Question for the authors. How were A1 spikes detected for the firing rates (0.47 and 0.57 Hz), and which periods count as spontaneous and evoked, in A1 and in MGB? The analysis code in the data set detects whole-cell spikes by hand, and its automatic detector for cell-attached data gives MGB evoked rates of 5.0 to 5.1 Hz (7.1 Hz with half its threshold) against 11.4 Hz.
The Results give 73 of 110 probes as 64.6% for frequency changes; 73/110 is 66.4%, and 64.6% is the AM proportion of the next sentence (62/96).

The paper's analysis script CxtDep.m centres each trial on its own mean over the probe period before computing the fractional powers, where the Methods centre the whole trace over time. It also counts silence as a context of every probe, which the Methods do not say. The attempt follows the script.

entries.name: asari-2009
entries.title: Long-lasting context dependence in rat auditory cortex (Asari & Zador 2009)
entries.description: Tests the findings of Asari and Zador (2009) on CRCNS ac-1, which holds their in vivo whole-cell recordings in rat A1 and cell-attached recordings in MGB, with natural and synthetic sound sequences, and the analysis code of the paper. It measures how long the response to a probe depends on the preceding sound, the response predictability without context, the dependence on sound properties, and the fast decay in thalamus. The voltage-clamp recordings of Figures 5 and 6 are not in the data set.
